subject: Svenska 3
title: Source handling and referencing technique
sourceSummary: In-text citation versus footnotes, the structure of a reference list, quotation versus paraphrase, and plagiarism and how to avoid it.

questions.prompt: What characterises in-text citation (e.g. the Harvard system) compared with the footnote system?
questions.opener: Where in the text does the source information end up — directly in the sentence, or at the bottom of the page?
choices: The source is given in brackets directly in the running text, e.g. (Andersson, 2020)
The source is never given in the text itself, only in the reference list
The source is indicated with a superscript number that refers to the bottom of the page
The source is only given in the introduction, once for the whole text
questions.explanation: With in-text citation, the author and year (and sometimes page) are written in brackets directly in the body text. The footnote system, by contrast, is the one that uses superscript numbers referring to notes at the bottom of the page.

questions.prompt: What is the most important advantage of the footnote system compared with in-text citation?
questions.opener: Consider what a bracket in the middle of a sentence does to reading flow, compared with a small number.
choices: It requires no reference list at all
It disrupts the flow of the body text less, while also allowing longer comments in the note
It is the only system approved in academic texts
It means you never need to state the year
questions.explanation: A small superscript number disrupts reading less than a bracket in the middle of a sentence, and the note can also include explanatory comments in addition to the source reference itself. Both systems require a reference list, and both are accepted conventions.

questions.prompt: Which order is usually used to sort sources in a reference list?
questions.opener: Consider how a library catalogue or a dictionary is sorted.
choices: By year of publication, oldest to newest
By the length of the text, shortest to longest
In the order the sources are first mentioned in the text
Alphabetically by the author's surname
questions.explanation: The reference list is normally sorted alphabetically by the author's surname (or by title if there is no author), which makes it easy for the reader to look up a particular source. Sorting by year or length is not used as the main principle.

questions.prompt: What is required for a quotation to be correctly reproduced?
questions.opener: How much are you allowed to change in the actual wording when quoting?
choices: The quotation should be briefly summarised in your own words
The quotation should be reproduced word for word, marked with quotation marks (or indentation for longer quotations), and given a source reference
The quotation may be freely shortened without this being indicated
The quotation needs no source reference if it is short
questions.explanation: A quotation should reproduce the source's exact wording, clearly marked and with a source reference. If parts of the quotation are removed, this should be indicated with [...]. Summarising in your own words is instead a paraphrase, not a quotation.

questions.opener: Compare with a summary: what is the similarity and what is the difference in scope?
choices: A word-for-word copy of a short passage of text without a source
A list of all the sources used
A rendering of a specific thought or sentence in your own words and your own sentence structure, with the meaning preserved
A summary of an entire book in a few sentences
questions.explanation: A paraphrase rephrases a delimited thought or passage in your own words and your own structure, but keeps the meaning — and, like a summary and a quotation, must be given a source reference. This differs from a full summary of an entire work, which is more a summary on a larger scale.

questions.prompt: Which of the following counts as plagiarism, even though the writer has not copied the text word for word?
questions.opener: It is not enough for the wording to differ if the source is missing or if the idea is presented as the writer's own.
choices: Quoting a sentence with quotation marks and a source reference
Reproducing an author's central idea in your own words but entirely without a source reference
Paraphrasing a passage and clearly stating where it comes from
Writing a summary with reporting markers and a reference list
questions.explanation: Plagiarism is not only about word-for-word copying but about presenting someone else's ideas, reasoning or findings as your own — even in your own words, it becomes plagiarism if the source is missing. The other options are correctly source-handled.

questions.prompt: Original quotation from an article by Berg (2021): "The increased screen time among teenagers has led to shorter sleep and worse concentration at school." Write both a correct quotation and a correct paraphrase of the sentence, both with a source reference according to the in-text system.
questions.opener: The quotation should be word for word and marked, the paraphrase should have its own words and its own sentence structure.
questions.answer: Quotation: Berg (2021) writes: "The increased screen time among teenagers has led to shorter sleep and worse concentration at school." Paraphrase: According to Berg (2021), teenagers' increased time in front of screens has contributed to them sleeping less and finding it harder to concentrate at school.
steps: For the quotation: keep the exact wording of the original and put quotation marks around it.
Add a clear source reference next to the quotation, e.g. "Berg (2021) writes:".
For the paraphrase: reword the content in your own words and with a different sentence structure from the original.
Check that the paraphrase preserves the original meaning without adding or removing information.
State the source for the paraphrase too, e.g. with "According to Berg (2021)" — paraphrases require a source reference just like quotations.

questions.prompt: Summarise in-text citation, the footnote system, quotation, paraphrase and plagiarism.
questions.opener: Sort the concepts by where the source ends up and how much of the original's wording is kept.
questions.answer: In-text citation: source in brackets in the body text, e.g. (Berg, 2021) · Footnote system: superscript number referring to a note at the bottom of the page, disrupts reading flow less · Quotation: word-for-word reproduction, quotation marks/indentation, always with a source · Paraphrase: rewording of a delimited thought in your own words, with a source · Summary: condensing longer content in your own words, with a source · Plagiarism: presenting other people's words or ideas as your own, regardless of whether the wording has been changed, when the source is missing · Reference list: sorted alphabetically by the author's surname.

questions.prompt: Which referencing system is best known for giving sources in the format (Surname, year) directly in the running text?
questions.opener: The system is named after an American university.
choices: The Harvard system (in-text citation)
The footnote system
A system with no source references at all
A system only used in fiction
questions.explanation: The Harvard system is a common name for the system of in-text citation, where author and year are given in brackets directly in the body text. The footnote system instead uses superscript numbers referring to notes at the bottom of the page.

questions.prompt: If a source has no stated author, how is it usually sorted in the reference list?
questions.opener: What is left to sort by when the author's name is missing?
choices: By the source's title
The source is left out of the list entirely
By publication year alone, regardless of title
The source is always placed last, regardless of letter
questions.explanation: If the author is missing, the source is instead sorted alphabetically by title. A source should never be omitted or placed last just because it lacks an author — it still needs to be findable in the list.

questions.prompt: If you quote a longer passage (several sentences), how is this often marked typographically, unlike a short quotation?
questions.opener: Think about how longer quotations are often set apart from the surrounding text.
choices: With indentation and/or a smaller font size, without quotation marks
By writing the whole quotation in capital letters
By never giving a source for longer quotations
By using italics only
questions.explanation: Longer quotations are often marked with indentation and sometimes a smaller font size, which makes quotation marks unnecessary since the indentation itself shows it is a quotation. A source reference is still required, just as for short quotations.

questions.prompt: What is a summary, as distinct from a paraphrase?
questions.opener: Compare the scope: a delimited thought, or an entire piece of content?
choices: A condensed account of longer content (e.g. a whole article) in your own words
A word-for-word copy without a source
Always shorter than a paraphrase
Another word for quotation
questions.explanation: A summary condenses longer content, such as a whole article or chapter, in your own words, while a paraphrase reworks a more limited thought or sentence. Both require a source reference, unlike a word-for-word copy without a source, which counts as plagiarism.

questions.prompt: If a student submits a text where large parts have been written by an AI service without this being stated, what does this usually count as?
questions.opener: Ask whether the reader can trust that the text reflects the student's own work.
choices: A form of academic dishonesty/plagiarism, since the work is not the student's own without this being made clear
A fully acceptable way of working, with no requirement to state the source
Irrelevant, since AI is not a "real" source
Only a problem if the teacher happens to notice
questions.explanation: Submitting AI-generated content as your own without stating it counts as a form of academic dishonesty, since the text then falsely appears to be the student's own work. That a source is new or unusual, like an AI service, does not exempt you from the requirement to state it.

questions.prompt: What do footnotes and entries in a reference list have in common?
questions.opener: Think about the basic purpose of all source handling.
choices: Both should allow the reader to trace where the information comes from
Both are always placed in the middle of the running text
Both are always written entirely in capital letters
Neither needs to include the author's name
questions.explanation: Both footnotes and entries in a reference list aim to let the reader trace and verify where the information comes from, even though they do so in somewhat different ways and in different places in the text.

questions.prompt: What is the best strategy for avoiding unintentional plagiarism when writing about other people's texts?
questions.opener: Think about what is always required, regardless of how you reproduce the information.
choices: Always stating the source, whether you are quoting, paraphrasing or summarising
Never reading any sources at all before writing
Swapping out a few individual words in the original text but keeping the sentence structure
Writing as quickly as possible without thinking about the sources
questions.explanation: Consistently stating the source, whether you quote, paraphrase or summarise, is the most fundamental strategy for avoiding plagiarism. Swapping out a few words but keeping the sentence structure still counts as plagiarism if the source is missing.
